title: Salary Sacrifice New Car: How It Fits Into Your Hourly to Annual Pay Conversion
description: Learn how to convert your hourly rate to annual pay, including tax, super, and salary sacrifice new car options. Understand the National Minimum Wage vs award rates.
salarySummary: For a full-time employee working 38 hours per week, annual gross pay is hourly rate × 38 × 52, with super paid on top.

faqs.q: How does a salary sacrifice new car affect my take-home pay?
faqs.a: A salary sacrifice new car arrangement lets you pay for a car from your pre-tax salary, reducing your taxable income. However, it also reduces your super guarantee base (ordinary earnings) and may affect leave entitlements. The calculator on this site does not include salary sacrifice; you should adjust your expected hourly rate or use the take-home pay estimate as a starting point. Always check with your employer or a financial adviser.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the National Minimum Wage and an award rate?
faqs.a: The National Minimum Wage, set by the Fair Work Commission, is the minimum base rate for employees not covered by an award or agreement. From 1 July 2026 it is $26.44 per hour for a 38-hour week. Award rates are industry- or occupation-specific minimums that are often higher. Many awards also include penalty rates, allowances, and overtime provisions. Your pay must meet whichever minimum applies to you.

faqs.q: How do I calculate my annual salary from an hourly rate if I work casual hours?
faqs.a: If you are a casual employee, your hourly rate typically includes a 25% casual loading on top of the base rate. To estimate annual gross pay, multiply your casual hourly rate by the average hours you work per week, then by 52. For a standard 38-hour week, that would be casual rate × 38 × 52. Remember that super is paid on your ordinary earnings (base rate plus casual loading) at 12% on top.

bodyMarkdown:
## From Hourly to Annual: A Practical Guide

Whether you are negotiating a salary, comparing job offers, or planning your finances, converting an hourly rate to an annual figure is a fundamental skill. This guide walks you through the formula, the assumptions behind it, and how factors like the National Minimum Wage, award rates, casual loading, and superannuation affect the numbers. We also look at how a **salary sacrifice new car** arrangement might change your calculations.

### The Basic Formula

The standard conversion is straightforward:

**Annual gross pay = hourly rate × hours per week × 52**

This assumes you work the same number of hours every week, with no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, and no allowances. For most full-time employees, the typical week is 38 hours, as defined by the Fair Work Ombudsman. If your hours differ, adjust accordingly. For example, a part-time worker on 20 hours per week would use 20 instead of 38.

To check your fortnightly pay, simply multiply your weekly pay by two. This can help when budgeting for bills that come every two weeks.

### National Minimum Wage vs Award Rates

The [National Minimum Wage](/topics/minimum-wage) is the legal floor. From 1 July 2026, it is $26.44 per hour, or $1,004.90 per week for a 38-hour week. However, most employees are covered by an award or enterprise agreement that sets higher minimum rates. Award rates vary by industry and occupation, and they often include additional payments for evening work, weekends, or public holidays.

If you are comparing a job offer, check the relevant [pay guides](/blog) or [reference tables](/data) to see the correct minimum. The hourly rate you enter into [the timesheet](/) should be your base rate before any casual loading or penalties.

### Casual Loading and Super

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate to compensate for lack of paid leave. The on-site calculator has a checkbox to add this loading automatically. **Never enter a rate that already includes casual loading** – let the tool add it for you.

Superannuation is paid on top of your ordinary earnings at 12% (the super guarantee rate for 2026–27). This means if your base hourly rate is $30.00, your employer must contribute an extra $3.60 per hour into your super fund, up to the maximum contribution base of $270,830 per year. The annual figure shown on this site is your gross pay before super; super is an additional benefit.

### Tax and Take-Home Pay

Once you have your annual gross pay, you can estimate your tax using the 2026–27 resident tax rates:

- Nil tax on the first $18,200
- 15% on income from $18,201 to $45,000
- 30% on income from $45,001 to $135,000
- 37% on income from $135,001 to $190,000
- 45% on income above $190,000

Plus the Medicare levy of 2% (based on 2025–26 single reduction thresholds, as 2026–27 thresholds were not confirmed). The [take-home pay](/topics/take-home) estimate on this site uses these rates but does not include HELP repayments, the Medicare levy surcharge, or salary packaging.

### Salary Sacrifice New Car: What It Means for Your Pay

A **salary sacrifice new car** arrangement allows you to pay for a vehicle (including running costs) from your pre-tax salary. This reduces your taxable income, which can lower the amount of tax you pay. However, it also reduces your ordinary earnings for super guarantee purposes, meaning your employer may pay less super. Additionally, salary sacrifice can affect your leave entitlements and other award conditions.

When using the hourly-to-annual conversion, remember that the calculator assumes no salary sacrifice. If you have a salary sacrifice new car agreement, your actual take-home pay will be different. You can adjust by entering a lower effective hourly rate that reflects the sacrificed amount, but it is best to consult a financial adviser or use the [super and packaging](/topics/super-and-packaging) resources for a more accurate picture.

### Averages vs Your Job

The on-site reference includes ABS Average Weekly Earnings for May 2026: full-time adult ordinary time $2,083.70 per week, and all employees total earnings $1,579.20 per week (including part-time). These are **averages**, not medians for a specific job. Do not assume your role pays the average. For job-specific data, refer to the [job pay](/topics/job-pay) section or consult industry sources.

### Putting It All Together

Let’s walk through an example. Suppose you are a full-time employee on the National Minimum Wage of $26.44 per hour, working 38 hours per week.

- Weekly pay: $26.44 × 38 = $1,004.72 (close to the official $1,004.90 due to rounding)
- Fortnightly pay: $1,004.72 × 2 = $2,009.44
- Annual gross: $26.44 × 38 × 52 = $52,245.44
- Super (12%): $6,269.45 on top (if below the maximum contribution base)
- Estimated tax (using 2026–27 rates): approximately $5,617 (including Medicare levy)
- Estimated take-home: around $46,628 per year

If you were casual, your rate would be $33.05 per hour (including 25% loading), giving:
- Annual gross: $33.05 × 38 × 52 = $65,306.80
- Super: $7,836.82 on top

Now, if you also had a **salary sacrifice new car** arrangement worth $10,000 per year, your taxable income would drop to about $55,306.80, reducing your tax but also lowering your super base. The exact impact depends on your employer’s policy and the type of salary sacrifice.

### Important Disclaimer

Annual pay shown here is hourly rate × hours per week × 52. It assumes the same rate every week, no unpaid overtime, no penalty rates, no allowances, and no salary sacrifice. Super is estimated at 12% of ordinary earnings only, paid on top, and stops at the $270,830 maximum contribution base. Tax is the 2026–27 resident scale with the full tax-free threshold. Medicare uses the 2025–26 single reduction thresholds because the 2026–27 reduction thresholds were not confirmed here. HELP, the Medicare levy surcharge, and salary packaging are not deducted. This is an estimate, not a determination of your pay or tax.

For more detailed calculations, use [the timesheet](/) and explore the [hourly conversion](/topics/hourly-conversion) and [casual loading](/topics/casual-loading) pages.
